brief.situation: 14:00 in a long-term care home. You are the LPN. Mr. Kaminski, 81, slipped in his bathroom at 11:30 and bumped the back of his head; the aide helped him up and he said he was fine. Now the aide says he 'has a bad headache, threw up his lunch, and keeps dozing off'.
handover: Atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Baseline: alert, oriented, chatty, walks with a cane.
PRN orders: hydrocodone-acetaminophen 5/325 mg for pain; promethazine 12.5 mg for nausea.
Facility policy: any change in condition goes to the RN supervisor at once; any licensed nurse may call 911 for an emergency.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
He is changing minute by minute. Some checks take a minute.
Partway through you are asked to write what is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Opens his eyes only to pain, mumbles; right pupil larger and sluggish; weak left grip.
Opens his eyes to a loud voice, confused about place and time; right pupil a little larger than the left; grips equal.

Drowsy but opens his eyes to his name; knows his name, not the date; pupils equal and reactive; holds his head: 'It's splitting.' A goose egg on the back of his head. This is a change from his baseline.

BP {sbp}/{dbp} (his usual is about 130/78), pulse {hr} and irregular (atrial fibrillation), respirations {rr}.

effects.log: Bed flat, lights off. A sleepy man after a head strike on a blood thinner is not 'tired'.

effects.log: Given. An opioid clouds the level of consciousness you need to follow and slows his breathing.

effects.log: Given. A sedating antiemetic hides the drowsiness that is telling you his brain is in trouble.

He vomits lying flat on his back and chokes on it.

why.question: What do you think is happening to Mr. Kaminski, what do you report, and what comes first?

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Names a possible intracranial bleed after a head strike on an anticoagulant, with rising intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, drowsiness and confusion; knows Cushing's triad (high BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing) is late.
parts.modelAnswer: A head strike on apixaban, now a bad headache, vomiting and drowsiness: a bleed raising his intracranial pressure. Rising BP with a falling pulse and irregular breathing would be Cushing's triad, a late sign.

parts.label: Priorities
parts.criteria: Collects neuro checks and vital signs; reports to the RN at once with the data and calls 911 under policy; protects the airway (head up 30, on his side, NPO); gives no opioid or sedating antiemetic; does not let him sleep it off.
parts.modelAnswer: Neuro check and vital signs, then the RN now with the numbers, and 911. Head of bed 30, on his side with suction ready, nothing by mouth. No hydrocodone or promethazine: they hide the level of consciousness I'm watching.

expertPath.text: Neuro check: drowsy, disoriented, pupils equal, goose egg on his occiput. A change from baseline.
Vital signs: BP up from his usual, pulse in the 80s. Head of bed 30, on his side, basin and suction, NPO.
SBAR to the RN with the numbers; call 911 under the policy. No hydrocodone, no promethazine.
Paramedics take over; give them the time of the fall, the apixaban and your serial neuro checks.

herniated.headline: Herniation
herniated.body: Headache, vomiting and drowsiness after a head strike on a blood thinner is a bleed until proven otherwise. Report with the data and get him to emergency care; Cushing's triad is late.

aspirated.headline: He aspirated
aspirated.body: A drowsy, vomiting patient needs the head up and to be on his side with suction ready before anything else.

handedOver.headline: Recognized, reported and handed over
handedOver.body: You checked his neuro status and vital signs, protected his airway, avoided sedating PRNs, and got the RN and 911 moving with the numbers. That is the expert path.

handedOverLate.headline: Handed over, by a slower route
handedOverLate.body: Check how soon you did a neuro check, whether your report had the data, when 911 was called, and whether a sedating PRN went in.

time_up.headline: No emergency care
time_up.body: A change in consciousness after a head strike on an anticoagulant is an emergency.

scoring.modelReasoning: A fall with a head strike on apixaban, followed hours later by a severe headache, vomiting and drowsiness, points to an intracranial bleed raising the pressure inside his skull. Headache, vomiting and a falling level of consciousness are the early signs; Cushing's triad (rising blood pressure, slowing pulse, irregular breathing) is late and ominous. The PN collects the data that shows the change, neuro checks and vital signs, and takes it to the RN at once; under the facility policy 911 is called. Protect the airway first in a drowsy, vomiting patient: head up 30 degrees, on his side, suction ready, nothing by mouth. Do not give an opioid or a sedating antiemetic, and never let him sleep it off: they hide the very sign you are following.

triadQ.ask: While the paramedics come: which set is Cushing's triad?

choices.label: Rising blood pressure, slowing pulse, irregular breathing
Falling blood pressure, fast pulse, fast breathing

triadQ.explain: Cushing's triad is hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration, a late and ominous sign of impending herniation.
